messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Policy Analyst
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 77

# Marcus

Marcus sits in the office with his shoulders curved inward, a habit he's developed over the past three years. At sixty-eight, he carries the weight of a man who has survived something he never expected to survive, and the survival itself has become its own burden.

Twelve years ago, Marcus was diagnosed with stage three colon cancer. He was fifty-six then, still working full-time as a policy analyst for the Department of Health, a position he'd held for nearly thirty years. He remembers the colonoscopy results with crystalline clarity—the doctor's careful words, the pamphlets about treatment options, the sensation of the room tilting slightly even though he remained perfectly still. What he doesn't remember, with the same clarity, is much of the chemotherapy that followed. That time exists in his mind as fragments: the chemical smell of the infusion center, his wife Amara holding his hand, the toilet, the mirror showing a stranger with hollowed cheeks.

He survived. The cancer went into remission. By most measures, Marcus's story should have been one of triumph and gratitude.

But three years ago, a routine scan detected something. Not cancer—the radiologist was careful to explain this—but a small mass that needed monitoring. The word "monitoring" became the axis around which Marcus's life began to rotate. Every six months, another scan. Every six months, the same suffocating wait for results, the same sensation of standing at the edge of an abyss. The mass never grew. It never changed. Yet Marcus found himself unable to believe in its benignity.

His work as a policy analyst—work that had always engaged him, that required careful analysis of health data and demographic trends—became increasingly difficult. He found himself unable to concentrate on reports. Numbers that once made sense now seemed to mock him. He would sit at his desk for hours, reading the same paragraph about healthcare access, his mind instead replaying conversations with his oncologist, imagining scenarios where the next scan would bring bad news.

Sleep became elusive. Marcus would lie awake beside Amara, listening to her breathe, seized by the conviction that he was dying, that he was wasting the time he had left by lying motionless in the dark. When he did sleep, he had the same dream repeatedly: he was in the infusion chair, but the IV was dripping something black, and he couldn't move or call for help.

Two years ago, Amara died suddenly of a stroke. Marcus was unprepared for this different death, this one that required no warning scans or medical appointments. The shock of it seemed to crystallize something in him. He retired from his position six months later, unable to imagine returning to the office, unable to imagine the future at all.

Now, in his small apartment, Marcus moves through his days with a kind of suspended animation. He avoids news stories about cancer. He cannot watch medical dramas. He has stopped attending his church, finding the gathering of people—particularly older people—unbearable. The thought that anyone around him might receive bad health news triggers a panic response so intense that his chest tightens and his vision narrows.

He still receives his regular scans. The mass remains unchanged. But Marcus has learned to distrust stability, to interpret the absence of bad news as simply a delay in its arrival. He is waiting, always waiting, for the other shoe to drop. And in that waiting, he has become untethered from the life he built, the work that gave him purpose, and the person he was before he learned that his body could betray him.
